'''''Cardamine hirsuta''''', commonly called '''hairy bittercress''', '''popping cress''',<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mpipz.mpg.de/4251574/pm_hay_2016_06|title=Exploding myths about seed dispersal|publisher=Max Planck Institute for Plant Breeding Research|date=2 June 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://asknature.org/strategy/what-puts-the-explosive-pop-in-popping-cress/|title=What Puts the Explosive Pop in Popping Cress?|date=May 16, 2021|last=Lippsett|first=Lonny|work=AskNature|publisher=[[The Biomimicry Institute]]}}</ref> '''common bittercress''', '''hoary bittercress''', '''hairy wood-cress''', '''small bittercress''', '''pepperweed''', '''shotweed''', or '''snapweed''',<ref>{{cite book|last=Quattrocchi|first=Umberto|title=CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymolog|url=https://archive.org/details/crc-world-dictionary-of-medicinal-and-poisonous-plants|publisher=CRC Press|edition=1st|year=2012|p=804|doi=10.1201/b16504|isbn=9781420080445}}</ref> is an annual or biennial species of plant in the family [[Brassicaceae]], and is edible<ref>{{cite book|author1=Horn, Dennis|author2=Duhl, David |author3=Ellsworth Hemmerly, Thomas|author4=Cathcart, Tavia|title=Wildflowers of Tennessee, the Ohio Valley, and the Southern Appalachians: the official field guide of the Tennessee Native Plant Society|year=2005|publisher=Lone Pine Publishers|location=Edmonton|isbn=978-1-55105-428-5|pages=112}}</ref> as a salad green. It is common in moist areas around the world.

==Description==
[[File:Cardamine hirsuta NRM.jpg|thumb|left|''Cardamine hirsuta'' flowers]]
[[File:Cardamine hirsuta (8691772885).jpg|thumb|left|Flowers and leaves]]
Depending on the climate ''C. hirsuta'' may complete two generations in a year, one in the spring and one in the fall; also depending on the climate, the seeds may [[germinate]] in the fall and the plants may remain green throughout the winter before flowering in the spring. It often grows a [[rosette (botany)|rosette]] of leaves at the base of the stem, while there may be leaves on the upright stem, most of the leaves will be part of the basal rosette. The leaves in this rosette are pinnately divided into 8–15 leaflets which have short stems connecting them to the petiole. These basal leaves are often {{Convert|3.5-15|cm|abbr=on}} long. The leaflets are round to ovate in shape and may have smooth or dentate edges. The leaflet at the tip of the leaf (terminal leaflet) will be larger than the other leaflets and round to [[Glossary of leaf morphology#reniform|reniform]] in shape. The cauline (attached to the upright stem) leaves are also pinnately divided, with fewer leaflets, and generally smaller than the basal leaves; these leaves will be borne on a [[petiole (botany)|petiole]] and are {{convert|1.2-5.5|cm|4=1|abbr=on}} long. The stems, petioles, and upper surfaces of the cauline leaves are sparsely hairy.

[[File:Cardamine hirsuta6pl.jpg|thumb|left|Fruits]]Plants of this species are usually erect and grow to no more than about {{convert|30|cm}} from a stem which is either unbranched or branched near the base.<ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles.'' Cambridge. University Press. {{ISBN|0521046564}}.</ref><ref name="efloras"/> The small white flowers are borne in a [[raceme]] without any bracts,<ref name="efloras"/> soon followed by the [[seed]]s and often continuing to flower as the first seeds ripen. The flowers have 4 white petals (which may be lacking but are mostly present)<ref>{{cite web|title=Taxon Page|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200009312|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=23 June 2016}}</ref> which are 1.5–4.5 mm long and [[spatulate]] shaped. The flowers also have 4 [[stamen]]s of equal height instead of the 6 which are found in most closely related plants. Pollen grains are elongated, approximately 32 microns in length.
[[File:碎米荠种子 Seed of Cardamine hirsuta.jpg|left|thumb|Seeds]]
Below the flowers there are 4 [[sepal]]s which are oblong shaped and 1.5–2.5 mm long and .3–.7 mm wide. The seeds are borne in upright pointing [[siliqua (plant)|siliquae]] which are straight and 1.5–2.5 cm long and 1–1.4'' ''mm in diameter. When the fruit is ripe the valves on the siliquae will coil tightly from the bottom to the top after being touched and [[explosive dehiscence|burst explosively]], sending the seeds flying far from the parent plant.<ref name="Rhoads-2007">{{cite book|last1=Rhoads|first1=Ann|last2=Block|first2=Timothy|title=The Plants of Pennsylvania|date=5 September 2007|publisher=University of Pennsylvania press|location=Philadelphia Pa|isbn=978-0-8122-4003-0|edition=2}}</ref> This seed dispersal strategy is referred to as [[ballochory]] and is a type of [[rapid plant movement]].

[[File:Pollens of Cardamine hirsuta.jpg|thumb|Pollen]]
Hairy bittercress is very similar to ''[[Cardamine flexuosa]]''. Some differences are that ''C. hirsuta'' stems are hairless and the leaves do not clasp the stems, as in ''C. flexuosa''. It usually has only 4 [[stamen]]s, while ''C. flexuosa'' has 6 stamens, and the fruits of ''C. hirsuta'' overtop the flowers whereas in ''C. flexuosa'' the fruits do not overtop the younger flowers. The fruits grow in a thin pod arranged as a single row.<ref>Webb, D.A., Parnell, J. and Doogue, D. 1996. Dundalgan Press Ltd. {{ISBN|0852211317}}.</ref><ref>Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora''. Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}.</ref>

''Cardamine hirsuta'' has a chromosome number of 2n = 16.<ref name="Marhold-1995">{{Cite journal|last=Marhold|first=Karol|date=1 June 1995|title=Taxonomy of the genus Cardamine L. (Cruciferae) in the Carpathians and Pannonia. III|journal=Folia Geobotanica|volume=30|issue=4|pages=397–434|doi=10.1007/BF02803971|s2cid=33850922|issn=1874-9348}}</ref>

==Habitat and distribution==
It is commonly found in damp, recently disturbed soil, open ground, turf and waste places<ref>{{cite book|last1=Rhoads|first1=Ann|last2=Block|first2=Timothy|title=The Plants of Pennsylvania|date=5 September 2007|publisher=University of Pennsylvania Press|location=Philadelphia Pa|isbn=978-0-8122-4003-0|edition=2nd}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|author-link=Clive A. Stace|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location=Cambridge, U.K.|isbn=9780521707725}}</ref>{{rp|401}} and native to Europe, the Middle East, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, North Africa, Central Africa, and the Horn of Africa.<ref>{{cite web|title=Cardamine hirsuta L.|work=Plants of the World Online|publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew|url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:280380-1|access-date=18 April 2024}}</ref>

These conditions are prevalent in nursery or garden centre plants, and hairy bittercress seeds may be introduced with those plants. Once established, it is difficult to eradicate. The tiny flowers are attractive to a few early butterflies, including (in the United States) spring azure (''[[Celastrina ladon]]'') and falcate orange-tip (''[[Anthocharis midea]]'').

''Cardamine hirsuta'' has been [[introduced species|introduced]] in many countries across the world. Its range includes but is not limited to: Argentina, Australia, Canada, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Gabon, Great Britain, India, Japan, Laos, Madagascar, Mexico, Pakistan, Panama, Peru, Philippines, South Africa, Sri Lanka, Thailand, Turkmenistan, United States, Venezuela, and Vietnam.<ref name="usda">{{cite web|title=Plants Profile for Cardamine hirsuta (hairy bittercress)|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=cahi3|website=plants.usda.gov|access-date=23 June 2016}}</ref><ref name="efloras">{{cite web|title=Taxon Page|url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200009312|website=www.efloras.org|access-date=23 June 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Tropicos {{!}} Name – !Cardamine hirsuta L.|url=http://www.tropicos.org/Name/4100096?tab=distribution|website=www.tropicos.org|access-date=23 June 2016}}</ref>

The 1889 book ''The Useful Native Plants of Australia'' records that it was also called "Lady's Smock" and that "This and other species afford excellent pot-herbs when luxuriant and flaccid. The present one is a common weed almost throughout the world."<ref>{{cite book|author=J. H. Maiden|year=1889|title=The useful native plants of Australia : Including Tasmania | publisher= Turner and Henderson, Sydney|url=https://primo-slnsw.hosted.exlibrisgroup.com/primo-explore/fulldisplay?docid=SLNSW_ALMA21105097830002626&context=L&vid=SLNSW&search_scope=EEA&tab=default_tab&lang=en_US}}</ref>

==Etymology and naming==
*Binomial etymology
**''Cardamine'' is [[Dioscorides]]' name for cress. It is derived from [[Greek language|Greek]].<ref name="Gledhill-2008">Gledhill, David (2008). "The Names of Plants". Cambridge University Press. {{ISBN|9780521866453}} (hardback), {{ISBN|9780521685535}} (paperback).  pp 91, 201.</ref>
**''Hirsuta'' means "hairy" or "hirsute".<ref name="Gledhill-2008"/>
*Common names
**Other common or country names include lamb's cress, land cress, hoary bitter cress, spring cress, flick weed, and shot weed, Alabama slapweed (or lambscress, landcress, hoary bittercress, springcress, flickweed, and shotweed). Some of these common names may be shared with other plants in the family [[Brassicaceae]], and are therefore of limited usefulness. As [[Old English]] ''stune'', the plant is cited as one of the herbs invoked in the [[Anglo-Saxon paganism|pagan Anglo-Saxon]] ''[[Nine Herbs Charm]]'', recorded in the 10th century.

==Uses==
The leaves, flowers, and seedpods are edible raw or cooked, and are said to have a mild peppery taste.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Nyerges|first=Christopher|title=Foraging Washington: Finding, Identifying, and Preparing Edible Wild Foods|publisher=Falcon Guides|year=2017|isbn=978-1-4930-2534-3|location=Guilford, CT|oclc=965922681}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Cardamine hirsuta (Bittercress, Flick Weed, Hairy Bittercress, Hoary Bittercress, Lamb's Cress, Land Cress, Shot Weed, Springcress) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/cardamine-hirsuta/|access-date=2024-03-24|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> In [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]] and [[Eastern Europe]], the leaves are used for salad, while seeds are a good substitute for [[Mustard (condiment)|mustard]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Ethnobotany of the Caucasus|editor-last1=Bussmann|editor-first1=Rainer W.|editor-last2=Paniagua-Zambrana|editor-first2=Narel Y.|editor-last3=Kikvidze|editor-first3=Zaal|year=2025|edition=2nd|p=1339|doi=10.1007/978-3-031-91369-3|isbn=978-3-031-91369-3}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Ethnobotany of the Caucasus|editor-last1=Bussmann|editor-first1=Rainer W.|editor-last2=Paniagua-Zambrana|editor-first2=Narel Y.|editor-last3=Kikvidze|editor-first3=Zaal|year=2025|edition=2nd|p=606|doi=10.1007/978-3-031-87802-2|isbn=978-3-031-87802-2}}</ref>
